225.title: What she hath done (Mark 14:1–11)
225.hook: the anointing at Bethany: what she did will be told wherever the gospel is preached
225.howItsDone: The Church reads the anointing at Bethany during Holy Week, and Catholic bishops bless the holy oils at the Chrism Mass that same week, the oils used for anointing at baptism, confirmation, ordination and for the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday, watch: no one knows the day or hour, so stay awake. Your line was finish today as if it matters. Today the passion begins, with a woman who was wide awake.

It's two days before Passover. In Jerusalem, the chief priests and scribes are looking for a quiet way to arrest Jesus and put him to death. Not during the feast, they say, or the people will riot. Just over the hill in Bethany, Jesus is at dinner in the house of Simon the leper. A woman walks in holding an alabaster jar of pure nard, very expensive. She doesn't open it. She breaks it, and pours it over his head. The room fills with the smell, and with outrage.
screen: `TWO DAYS BEFORE PASSOVER.` → `A DINNER IN BETHANY.` → `SHE BREAKS THE JAR.`

segments.voice: First, the complaint. Some at the table are indignant. What a waste! It could have been sold for more than three hundred pence, the Douay-Rheims says, and given to the poor. It sounds reasonable, even holy. Second, Jesus defends her: "Let her alone, why do you molest her? She hath wrought a good work upon me." You'll always have the poor with you, he says, and can do them good whenever you want. You won't always have me. "She hath done what she could: she is come beforehand to anoint my body for the burial." She seems to understand what the disciples still don't: he's going to die. Third, the anointing. Christ means the anointed one. In the old story, Samuel pours oil on Saul's head to make him king. Here, in a friend's house, a woman pours oil on Jesus's head. Not a priest. Not an apostle. Her. Fourth, the promise: "wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, that also which she hath done, shall be told for a memory of her." And here it is, told again, in your ears. Then look what Mark puts right beside her. Judas, one of the twelve, goes to the chief priests to hand Jesus over, and they promise him money. She's unnamed, and remembered for pouring out something precious. He's named, and selling someone precious. John's Gospel tells a similar anointing and names the woman Mary of Bethany. Mark lets her stay nameless, and remembered anyway.

segments.voice: Think of someone who did something good that nobody noticed: a coworker who covered for you, a neighbor who shoveled your walk, a grandparent who quietly held a family together. Let their face come to mind, remember exactly what they did, and think of who you could tell, so it's told for a memory of them. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name.
Memory. The promise Jesus makes about the woman who broke the jar at Bethany: wherever the gospel is preached, this will be told for a memory of her. Today's word.

226.title: The upper room (Mark 14:12–31)
226.hook: take, this is my body; this is my blood of the new testament
226.howItsDone: At every Catholic Mass the priest repeats Jesus's words over the bread and wine at the consecration, and Catholics receive Communion believing it is truly the body and blood of Christ; the Last Supper is remembered especially on Holy Thursday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, memory: a woman broke a jar of perfume over Jesus's head, and he promised she'd be remembered wherever the gospel goes. Your line was she did what she could. Today, supper.

It's the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lambs are sacrificed. Where should we get the meal ready, the disciples ask. Jesus sends two of them into the city with odd directions: you'll meet a man carrying a jar of water. Follow him. Ask the owner of the house he enters for the guest room, and he'll show you a large upper room, furnished and ready. It all happens just as he said. That evening Jesus arrives with the twelve. Catholics trace every Mass back to what happens at this table.
screen: `THE DAY OF THE PASSOVER LAMBS.` → `FOLLOW THE MAN WITH THE WATER JAR.` → `A LARGE UPPER ROOM, READY.`

segments.voice: First, the betrayal. While they're eating, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "one of you that eateth with me shall betray me." Heartbroken, one by one, they ask him: "Is it I?" Nobody points at anyone else. Second, the bread. "And whilst they were eating, Jesus took bread; and blessing, broke, and gave to them, and said: Take ye. This is my body." Took, blessed, broke, gave: almost the same four actions Mark used at the two feedings in the wilderness, and some readers hear those baskets echo here. Third, the cup. He gives thanks, and they all drink from it. "This is my blood of the new testament, which shall be shed for many." Testament here means covenant, a binding promise. At Sinai, Moses sealed God's covenant with blood. Now Jesus speaks of his own. Fourth, what Catholics believe. The Catholic Church teaches that at every Mass, when the priest speaks these words over bread and wine, they truly become the body and blood of Christ, while still looking like bread and wine. It calls this transubstantiation. Orthodox Christians also believe in a real change, and speak of it as a mystery; many Protestants understand the meal as a memorial or a spiritual presence. And notice the first word over the bread: take. In Mark, the bread is given to be received. Then they sing a hymn and walk out to the Mount of Olives, and Peter promises: "Although all shall be scandalized in thee, yet not I." Before the cock crows twice, Jesus tells him, you'll deny me three times.

segments.voice: Picture that room: low tables, lamplight, thirteen people close together, the smell of bread. Then picture your next meal, and one breath before it to remember this table. If you pray, you can say grace, or simply thank you; if you don't, just notice the bread in your hands and who made it.
Transubstantiation. What Catholics believe happens at Mass when the priest repeats Jesus's words over bread and wine: they truly become his body and blood. Today's word.
Your line: take. Bread, broken and given. That's day two hundred twenty-six.

227.title: Abba (Mark 14:32–52)
227.hook: he calls God by the family word, and a young man flees leaving his linen cloth
227.howItsDone: On Holy Thursday night many Catholic parishes keep watch before the Blessed Sacrament until midnight, remembering Jesus's prayer in Gethsemane, and the Agony in the Garden is the first Sorrowful Mystery of the rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, transubstantiation: bread and cup, and one word, take. After supper they walked out to the Mount of Olives. Today, the garden.

Most of us have had one night we'd never want to live again. Waiting for a phone call. Sitting by a bed. Today is that night for Jesus. They come to Gethsemane, an olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives; the name probably means oil press. He tells most of the disciples to sit and wait, takes Peter, James and John further in, and Mark says he began to be terrified and deeply troubled. My soul is sorrowful even unto death, he tells them. Stay here and watch. Then he goes a little further alone, and falls on the ground.
screen: `THE WORST NIGHT.` → `GETHSEMANE: THE OIL PRESS.` → `HE FALLS ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Face down in the dirt, he prays, in the Douay-Rheims: "Abba, Father, all things are possible to thee: remove this chalice from me; but not what I will, but what thou wilt." Abba is Aramaic, the everyday word for father inside a family. Mark keeps the sound, then translates it. You'll sometimes hear that abba means daddy. Scholars now say that's too cute: grown children called their fathers abba too. It's close, trusting, family speech, at the worst moment of his life. Second, the honesty. He asks for the cup to pass; he doesn't pretend to want it. Then he hands the choice back: not my will, yours. Catholics see here both his true human fear and his free obedience. Third, the sleepers. Three times he comes back and finds them asleep, two days after his speech ended on one word: watch. "Watch ye, and pray that you enter not into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh weak." Fourth, the arrest. Judas arrives with a crowd carrying swords and clubs, and greets Jesus with a kiss. Someone draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant. And then, Mark says, they all left him and fled. One detail only Mark tells: a young man following, wearing only a linen cloth. They grab him, and he leaves the cloth in their hands and runs away naked. Nobody knows who he was. An old guess says it was Mark himself, signing his Gospel. The sources don't say.
screen: `ABBA: THE FAMILY WORD FOR FATHER.` · `REMOVE THIS CHALICE. NOT MY WILL.` · `ASLEEP THREE TIMES. WATCH AND PRAY.` · `A KISS, A SWORD, AND THEY ALL FLED.` · then, large: `ABBA, FATHER, ALL THINGS ARE POSSIBLE TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the thing you most wish would pass from you right now, and say honestly that you don't want it. If you pray, you can use Jesus's own two words, Abba, Father, slowly, on your breath, as many times as you need. If you don't, think of the person whose voice feels most like home, and rest in that for a minute.
Abba. Aramaic for father, the word used inside a family. Jesus says it face down in Gethsemane, the night before he dies. Today's word.
Your line: abba, father. Fear and trust, in the same breath. See you tomorrow.

228.title: Before the cock crows twice (Mark 14:53–72)
228.hook: Jesus is silent before the council; Peter weeps
228.howItsDone: Catholics bring their sins to the sacrament of confession, and Peter's denial and tears are often held up in Catholic preaching as a picture of sorrow that leads back to mercy rather than despair.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abba: Jesus face down in the garden, calling God by the family word. Your line was abba, father. After the arrest, everyone fled. Almost everyone.

Three denials, spoken by a fire in the dark. Each one is said to protect himself, by the man who swore, only hours before, that he would never fall away. In the middle of the night they take Jesus to the high priest's house, where the chief priests and elders gather. And Peter, who ran away with the others, comes back. He follows at a distance, right into the courtyard, and sits with the servants, warming himself by the fire. Upstairs, a trial. Downstairs, by the fire, another one.
screen: `THREE DENIALS BY A FIRE.` → `PETER FOLLOWS AT A DISTANCE.` → `TWO TRIALS AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: First, the silence. Inside, witnesses accuse Jesus, but their stories don't agree. The high priest stands up and demands an answer. In the Douay-Rheims: "But he held his peace, and answered nothing." Jesus, who's been talking all through Mark, says nothing to the accusations. Second, the answer. The high priest asks him straight: are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? And Jesus, with no hedging at all: "I am." You shall see the Son of man at the right hand of power. It's called blasphemy, and some begin to spit on him and strike him. Third, the fire. Downstairs, a servant girl looks at Peter in the firelight: you were with the Nazarene. He says he doesn't know what she means. She tells the others; he denies it again. Then the bystanders: surely you're one of them. You're a Galilean. And Peter begins to curse and swear: "I know not this man of whom you speak." Upstairs, Jesus says I am. Downstairs, Peter says I'm not. Fourth, the tears. "And immediately the cock crew again." Peter remembers the word, before the cock crow twice, thou shalt thrice deny me. "And he began to weep." An early tradition, from a bishop named Papias, says Mark wrote down what Peter preached. If that's right, this story most likely came from Peter's own mouth. The man Catholics call the first pope told it on himself, and the Gospel kept it.
screen: `HE HELD HIS PEACE.` · `ARE YOU THE CHRIST? I AM.` · `BY THE FIRE: I KNOW NOT THIS MAN.` · `THE COCK CROWS, AND PETER WEEPS.` · then, large: `AND HE BEGAN TO WEEP.`

segments.voice: Bring back one moment you've regretted, when you protected yourself and someone else paid for it, and just remember it, the way Peter remembered the word: don't relive the details, don't defend yourself. If tears come, let them; if not, let there be quiet, because being sorry is not the same as being finished, and Peter's story didn't end by the fire. If you pray, you can bring that moment to God.
Blasphemy. What the high priest calls it when Jesus answers the elders plainly, I am, just before Peter, downstairs, denies him three times. Today's word.
Your line: peter wept. The rooster crowed, and he remembered. Day two hundred twenty-eight, done.

229.title: The crown (Mark 15:1–20)
229.hook: Barabbas released, the purple cloak, the crown of thorns
229.howItsDone: Catholics meditate on the crowning with thorns as the third Sorrowful Mystery of the rosary, and visiting the imprisoned is one of the Church's corporal works of mercy, carried out through prison ministries in many dioceses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, blasphemy: Jesus answered I am before the council, and Peter wept by the fire. Now it's morning, and Jesus is handed to Rome.

Early in the morning, the chief priests, the elders and the scribes hold a council, bind Jesus, and hand him over to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. The sentence will be his to give. Pilate has a custom at the feast: he releases one prisoner, whoever the crowd asks for. In his jail is Barabbas, locked up with rebels who committed murder in an uprising. Pilate offers the crowd a choice: Jesus, or Barabbas? And before long, soldiers will put a crown on Jesus's head. Not gold.
screen: `HANDED OVER TO PILATE.` → `JESUS, OR BARABBAS?` → `A CROWN, NOT OF GOLD.`

segments.voice: First, Pilate's question, in the Douay-Rheims: "Art thou the king of the Jews?" Jesus answers: "Thou sayest it." Then he's silent again while the chief priests accuse him of many things, and Pilate marvels. Second, the choice. Pilate seems to see that the charge comes out of envy. But the chief priests stir up the crowd to ask for Barabbas. What shall I do with this king, then? Crucify him. Wanting to satisfy the crowd, Pilate releases Barabbas, has Jesus scourged, and hands him over to be crucified. Some readers hear something in the prisoner's name: bar abba, Aramaic for son of the father, and last night Jesus called God Abba. If that's right, one son of the father walks free this morning, and the other takes his place. Third, the crown. Roman soldiers lead him into the governor's palace and call together the whole cohort. "And they clothe him with purple, and platting a crown of thorns, they put it upon him. And they began to salute him: Hail, king of the Jews." Purple is a king's color; that's the joke. They hit his head with a reed, spit on him, and kneel in mock worship. Fourth, the irony. They mean every piece as a joke: the purple cloak, the crown, the salute, the kneeling. In Mark's telling, every piece is true: he really is the king, and the soldiers are acting out a coronation without knowing it. Catholics remember this scene in the rosary, the third Sorrowful Mystery, the crowning with thorns. It was Rome's soldiers who mocked him, and Rome that crucified him.
screen: `ART THOU THE KING? THOU SAYEST IT.` · `JESUS, OR BARABBAS?` · `PURPLE, THORNS, HAIL, KING.` · `A CORONATION THEY DON'T UNDERSTAND.` · then, large: `AND PLATTING A CROWN OF THORNS.`

segments.voice: Jesus was a prisoner that morning: bound, mocked, beaten, with no one to speak for him. People sit in prison cells right now, some guilty, some not, some forgotten by everyone; bring one to mind, or picture a cell and someone in it this morning. If you pray, you can pray for them and for the people who guard them; if you don't, simply hold them in mind for a minute.
The crown. The crown of thorns Roman soldiers pressed on Jesus's head, hailing him as king. Today's word.
Your line: they mocked the king. Thorns for a crown. Until tomorrow.

230.title: Truly this man (Mark 15:21–47)
230.hook: Simon carries the cross, the centurion says Indeed this man was the son of God
230.tomorrow: Camp 4 close: he goes before you
230.howItsDone: Catholics walk the fourteen Stations of the Cross, especially on Fridays in Lent, where Simon of Cyrene helps Jesus carry the cross at the fifth station, and on Good Friday the passion is read aloud and the faithful venerate the cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crown: purple, thorns, and soldiers kneeling in mockery. Today, one of those soldiers sees something.

Roman soldiers grab a man coming in from the countryside and force him to carry a condemned man's cross. His name is Simon, from Cyrene, in North Africa. Mark adds that he was the father of Alexander and Rufus, as if his readers knew them. Maybe they did. Maybe carrying that cross changed a family. And at the end of the road, at Golgotha, the place of the skull, a Roman officer will say the sentence Mark has been building toward since his first line.
screen: `SIMON OF CYRENE, GRABBED.` → `THE FATHER OF ALEXANDER AND RUFUS.` → `GOLGOTHA, THE PLACE OF THE SKULL.`

segments.voice: First, the cross. They crucify him at the third hour, between two thieves. Over him, the charge: the King of the Jews. Passersby, priests, even the men crucified beside him mock him: he saved others, himself he cannot save. They're right, in a way they don't understand. Second, the cry. From the sixth hour darkness covers the land until the ninth. Jesus cries out in Aramaic, and Mark keeps the words: "Eloi, Eloi, lamma sabacthani? Which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" It's the first line of Psalm 21 in the Douay, 22 in most Bibles, a psalm this path met in camp four, which begins in abandonment and ends in praise. With a loud cry, he dies. The veil of the Temple is torn in two, top to bottom. Third, the soldier. Mark began his Gospel calling Jesus the Son of God. A voice from heaven has said it. Demons have shouted it. But in Mark, no human being has said it and meant it, until now. The centurion facing the cross sees how he died, and says: "Indeed this man was the son of God." A Roman, a Gentile, the officer in charge of the execution. Fourth, who stayed. The men have all fled. But women were watching from a distance: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, Salome, and many others who had followed him from Galilee. Then Joseph of Arimathea, a respected council member, goes boldly to Pilate, asks for the body, wraps it in linen, lays it in a tomb cut from rock, and rolls a stone across the door.
screen: `HE SAVED OTHERS, HIMSELF HE CANNOT.` · `MY GOD, MY GOD: PSALM 21 [22].` · `A ROMAN SOLDIER SAYS IT.` · `THE WOMEN STAYED.` · then, large: `INDEED THIS MAN WAS THE SON OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Simon didn't choose that cross; it was put on his shoulders on an ordinary day. Think of someone near you carrying something heavy right now, an illness, a move, a sick parent, a lot of work, a grief, and picture one piece of it you could carry for a while: a meal, an errand, an hour, a text that says I'm thinking of you. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

231.title: Camp 4 close: he goes before you (Mark 16)
231.hook: the women at the tomb hear he goes before you into Galilee
231.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the resurrection at the Easter Vigil and on every Sunday, and the resurrection is the first Glorious Mystery of the rosary; Mark 16 is read at the Easter Vigil in the year of Mark.

segments.voice: Yesterday, centurion: a Roman soldier at the cross said indeed this man was the son of God. Today camp four ends, at an empty tomb.

Very early on the first day of the week, with the sun now risen, three women walk to the tomb with spices to anoint the body: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome. They had watched the crucifixion from a distance. On the way they worry about something practical: who will roll the stone away for us? It was very big. They're not expecting a miracle; they're expecting a heavy rock and a dead friend. Then they look up, and the stone is already rolled back.
screen: `SUNRISE, THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.` → `WHO WILL ROLL THE STONE AWAY?` → `IT'S ALREADY ROLLED BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the news. Inside, a young man in a white robe is sitting on the right, and they're terrified. He says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Be not affrighted; you seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified: he is risen, he is not here." Second, the errand: "But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he goeth before you into Galilee; there you shall see him, as he told you." And Peter: the one who wept by the fire, named on purpose. Galilee is where it all began: the lake, the boats, the ordinary towns. He's not waiting in the Temple. He's gone ahead, back to the everyday. Third, the ending. The women run from the tomb, trembling, "and they said nothing to any man; for they were afraid." In some of the oldest manuscripts that survive, Mark stops right there. Later manuscripts carry a longer ending, with the risen Jesus appearing first to Mary Magdalene and sending the eleven out to the whole world. The Catholic Church receives that longer ending as inspired Scripture, and scholars still debate who wrote it and when. Either way, the story didn't stay untold. You're hearing it. Fourth, look back. This camp was the text itself. The Psalms: two ways, the Lord ruleth me, be still, have mercy, out of the depths, let every spirit praise. Then Mark straight through: the beginning, fishers of men, the sower, peace be still, Ephphatha, who do you say I am, Bartimaeus, the widow's mites, Abba, truly this man. Tomorrow a new camp begins, the depths, starting with how Catholics pray when words run out.
